I have been coaching people through second languages for about fifteen years, and there is one month I can predict without knowing anything about the student. It is usually the fourth. Everything before it feels wonderful. In the first two months every single lesson gives you something you could not do the week before, and that is not because you are brilliant. It is because almost everything was missing, so almost anything you add is visible. Then the basics are in place, the gains get smaller, and the whole thing levels off. That is the month people tell me they have stopped improving, and it is the month most of them quit. What I try to explain, and I am not always successful, is that a plateau is not a signal that something has gone wrong. It is what improvement looks like once it becomes incremental. You are still getting better. You have simply lost the ability to feel it, because the changes are now smaller than the difference between a good day and a bad day. So I ask every student to keep one thing: a written record of something specific they could not do a month ago. Not a feeling, a sentence. And the students who keep that record are, almost without exception, the ones who are still here a year later.

A study that gets quoted a great deal in this area followed two groups of adult learners for six months. Same material, same schedule, same teachers, and only one difference between them. The first group turned up and studied. The second group turned up, studied, and then wrote down a single number at the end of every session. It did not much matter which number, as long as it was the same one every time. Six months later, the second group was far more likely to still be attending, and the gap did not open up at the beginning. It opened at exactly the point where progress stopped being obvious, which was somewhere around the fourth month. The researchers were fairly careful about the explanation. They did not think the second group was more motivated, because motivation was measured at the start and the two groups were the same. What they suggested is much simpler and, I think, more useful. Without a record, the only thing you can compare today with is how you remember feeling last week, and nobody remembers that accurately. With a record, you compare it with something written down. The number is not the point. Having something outside your own head to argue with is the point.
